lead: Static CMOS builds every gate from two complementary networks: an nMOS pull-down network (PDN) that connects the output to ground and a pMOS pull-up network (PUN) that connects it to V<sub>DD</sub>. For every input combination exactly one of them conducts, so the output always sits at a rail and no steady current flows. Ratioed logic keeps the pull-down network but replaces the pull-up with one always-on load. It saves transistors, but its low output sits above 0 V and it draws current whenever the output is low. Static CMOS is the default style of standard-cell libraries.
prereq: You need: the CMOS inverter, the pseudo-nMOS load and logical effort.

items: Write the function in inverted form, Y = NOT(F). Static CMOS gates are inverting.
Build the PDN from F: an AND becomes nMOS in series, an OR becomes nMOS in parallel.
Build the PUN as the dual: every series connection in the PDN becomes parallel in the PUN, and every parallel one becomes series. The pMOS take the same inputs.
Size for the same drive as a unit inverter (nMOS 1, pMOS 2): a device in a stack of k gets k times the unit width.
Check each input's logical effort, and draw the stick diagram with an Euler path so one diffusion strip serves each network (see Stick diagrams).

blocks.text: A simple N-input gate uses 2N transistors. Because one network is always off in steady state, V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>, V<sub>OL</sub> = 0 V, static current is only leakage, and the noise margins are those of the inverter. The costs are the transistor count and the input capacitance of the series pMOS, which grow quickly for wide NOR gates; this is why gates are kept to about four inputs and larger functions are built as trees.
Some syllabi call this style complementary CMOS. It gives compound gates such as AND-OR-INVERT (AOI) and OR-AND-INVERT (OAI) in one stage.

In pseudo-nMOS the PUN is a single pMOS with its gate at ground. An N-input gate needs N + 1 transistors. When the PDN is off the load pulls the output to V<sub>DD</sub>. When the PDN is on, the load and the PDN both conduct, so a static current flows and the output settles at a V<sub>OL</sub> above 0 V set by the ratio of their strengths. For a NOR, the worst case is a single conducting nMOS, so each nMOS is sized to hold V<sub>OL</sub> on its own.

The load current is (k<sub>p</sub>/2)(V<sub>DD</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|)² while the pMOS stays saturated, which needs V<sub>OL</sub> ≤ |V<sub>tp</sub>|. Making k<sub>p</sub> small lowers V<sub>OL</sub> and the static current but slows the rising edge, so a pseudo-nMOS gate is fast falling and slow rising. Its logical effort for a falling output is low (an input drives only one nMOS), which is why wide pseudo-nMOS NOR gates appear in PLA planes, ROM address decoders and comparators.

A tristate inverter adds an enable nMOS and pMOS in series with the two networks; when disabled both paths are open and the output floats (high impedance), so several drivers can share a bus. Clocked CMOS (C²MOS) puts clock-driven transistors in series in the same way, so the gate follows its input only while the clock enables it; it is used in latches (see Static and dynamic latches and registers). Neither is ratioed, because neither has an always-on load. Pass-transistor and dynamic styles come in the next two chapters.

examples.question: Design the static CMOS gate Y = NOT(A·(B + C)). Give the PDN and PUN, size every transistor for the drive of a unit inverter (nMOS 1, pMOS 2), and find the logical effort of each input.
steps: F = A·(B + C). PDN: nMOS B and C in parallel, that pair in series with nMOS A, between Y and ground.
PUN (dual): pMOS B and C in series, that pair in parallel with pMOS A, between V<sub>DD</sub> and Y.
Check one case: A = 1, B = 0, C = 1. PDN: A on and C on, a path to ground, so Y = 0. PUN: pMOS A is off, and the B-C series pair has C off, so no path to V<sub>DD</sub>. Y = NOT(1·(0 + 1)) = 0. ✓
nMOS sizes: the worst pull-down path is two in series (A then B, or A then C), so each nMOS is width 2.
pMOS sizes: pMOS A alone forms a path, so width 2; B and C are two in series, so width 4 each.
Logical effort: input A drives nMOS 2 + pMOS 2 = 4 units, g<sub>A</sub> = 4/3. Inputs B and C drive 2 + 4 = 6 units, g<sub>B</sub> = g<sub>C</sub> = 6/3 = 2.
Count: 6 transistors. Built from separate gates it would need a NOR2, an inverter and a NAND2: 4 + 2 + 4 = 10 transistors and three gate delays instead of one.
examples.answer: PDN: A in series with (B ∥ C), all nMOS width 2. PUN: A ∥ (B in series with C), pMOS A width 2, B and C width 4. g<sub>A</sub> = 4/3, g<sub>B</sub> = g<sub>C</sub> = 2.

examples.question: A pseudo-nMOS inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 2.5 V, k<sub>n</sub> = 100 µA/V², V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.5 V, k<sub>p</sub> = 20 µA/V² and |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.5 V. With the input high, find the load current, V<sub>OL</sub> and the static power, and check that the pMOS is saturated.
steps: pMOS: V<sub>SG</sub> = 2.5 V, overdrive 2.0 V. Assume saturation: I = (20/2)(2.0)² = 40 µA.
nMOS: V<sub>GS</sub> = 2.5 V, overdrive 2.0 V, linear because V<sub>OL</sub> is small: 40 = 100[2.0V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2].
0.4 = 2V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2, so V<sub>OL</sub>² − 4V<sub>OL</sub> + 0.8 = 0 and V<sub>OL</sub> = (4 − √12.8)/2 = (4 − 3.578)/2 = 0.211 V.
Saturation check: V<sub>OL</sub> = 0.211 V ≤ |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.5 V, so the pMOS is saturated. ✓
Static power with the output low: 2.5 V × 40 µA = 100 µW.
examples.answer: I = 40 µA, V<sub>OL</sub> ≈ 0.21 V, static power 100 µW while the output is low.

traps: Drawing the PUN with the same series and parallel structure as the PDN. The PUN is the dual.
Forgetting that a static CMOS gate inverts. NOT(A·(B + C)) is one gate; A·(B + C) needs an inverter after it.
Sizing all transistors equally. Devices in a stack of k are made k times wider to keep the drive.
Saying a ratioed gate has zero static power. It draws V<sub>DD</sub> × I<sub>load</sub> whenever its output is low.
Sizing a pseudo-nMOS NOR for all inputs on. The worst case is one input on.

quiz.q: What are the two networks of a static CMOS gate and which transistors form each?
quiz.a: An nMOS pull-down network to ground and a pMOS pull-up network to V<sub>DD</sub>; they are duals, and exactly one conducts for each input.

quiz.q: Why does static CMOS draw no steady current?
quiz.a: For any steady input one network is off, so there is no path from V<sub>DD</sub> to ground; only leakage flows.

quiz.q: Draw the PDN and PUN of Y = NOT(A·B + C) and size them for unit-inverter drive.
quiz.a: PDN: (A series B) parallel with C; A and B width 2, C width 1. PUN: (A ∥ B) in series with C; all three pMOS width 4.

quiz.q: A pseudo-nMOS gate has k<sub>p</sub> = 40 µA/V², V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V and |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.4 V. Find the load current.
What is a tristate inverter used for?
quiz.a: It drives a shared bus: when its enable is off both paths open and the output floats, so another driver can take the bus.

quiz.q: A 16-input NOR is needed in a decoder. Compare static CMOS and pseudo-nMOS.
quiz.a: Static CMOS needs 32 transistors with 16 pMOS in series, each very wide, giving a huge input capacitance and a slow rise. Pseudo-nMOS needs 17 transistors and each input drives only one nMOS, but it burns static current whenever the output is low and has a reduced low noise margin.

quiz.q: In the pseudo-nMOS example, k<sub>p</sub> is doubled to 40 µA/V². Find the new V<sub>OL</sub> and comment.
quiz.a: I = 80 µA, so 0.8 = 2V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2, V<sub>OL</sub>² − 4V<sub>OL</sub> + 1.6 = 0, V<sub>OL</sub> = (4 − √9.6)/2 = 0.451 V. The pMOS is still saturated (0.451 ≤ 0.5). The rising edge is faster, but V<sub>OL</sub> doubles and the static power doubles to 200 µW.

beyond: Not for the exam. A standard-cell library offers hundreds of static CMOS cells, including many AOI and OAI compound gates in several drive strengths; synthesis maps logic onto them. Ratioed pull-ups survive in SRAM sense amplifiers and in fast comparators. Search next for AOI and OAI cells, Euler path layout and standard-cell libraries.

figure.caption: The six-transistor gate Y = NOT(A·(B + C)) of the worked example, with each width chosen for the drive of a unit inverter. The pull-up is the dual of the pull-down: the series pair B, C becomes a parallel pair below the output.
